message.content:
During the 19th century the world’s eyes were drawn most strongly to **Auguste Rodin’s “The Thinker”** (originally conceived in the 1880s, first cast in 1902). Even though its first public casts appeared just after the century closed, the work had already become emblematic of modern sculpture by the late 1800s, and it remains the most instantly recognizable 19th‑century piece today.

Other sculptures that rivaled it in fame at the time include:

| Sculpture | Artist | Year | Why it mattered |
|-----------|--------|------|-----------------|
| **“The Kiss”** | Rodin | 1889 | A sensual, almost erotic depiction that challenged Victorian norms and became a symbol of romantic love. |
| **“The Gates of Hell”** | Rodin | 1880–1890 | An ambitious monumental project that pushed the limits of bronze casting and narrative sculpture. |
| **“The Birth of Venus”** (modern reinterpretation) | Various artists | 19th‑century revivals | A revival of Renaissance iconography that captured the era’s fascination with classical themes. |

In short, while several works were celebrated in their own right, Rodin’s “The Thinker” stands out as the single most famous sculpture of the 19th century—its influence on both contemporary audiences and later generations is unmatched.
